slides.title: Definitions And Facts On Lie Algebras
slides.notes: Open the lecture by saying that this appendix is not a detached algebra review. It is the compact control panel used later for symmetric spaces, compact transformation groups, and homogeneous geometry. The main promise is that filtrations, bilinear forms, and decompositions let us read geometric rigidity from algebraic structure.

slides.title: Route Through The Appendix
slides.notes: Use this route slide to keep the appendix from feeling like a list of definitions. The source compresses many standard facts, so the lecture will organize them by use. We begin with commutator series, turn those into taxonomy, then use forms and decompositions to support later geometry.

slides.title: Two Ways To Descend By Brackets
slides.notes: Spend time distinguishing the two recursions. The derived series brackets a stage with itself, so it asks how non-abelian that stage remains. The central series brackets the whole algebra with the current stage, so it measures persistence under all adjoint actions from the original algebra.

slides.title: Taxonomy From Vanishing
slides.notes: This slide turns the bracket series into vocabulary. Make clear that the radical and nilradical are not arbitrary choices; they are maximum ideals with the stated behavior. This maximum property is what lets later arguments speak about the radical invariantly under automorphisms and quotients.

slides.title: Radical, Semi-Simple, Simple
slides.notes: Explain the radical as the largest solvable piece that cannot be ignored if one wants a faithful structure theorem. Semi-simple does not mean every subalgebra is simple; it means the solvable radical has disappeared. Simple is the indecomposable non-abelian case inside the semi-simple world.

slides.title: The Killing-Cartan Form
slides.notes: Present the Killing-Cartan form as a way of turning adjoint action into measurable linear algebra. The formula is simple, but its power comes from invariance. Orthogonal complements of ideals remain ideals, so nondegeneracy is not just metric language; it is structural information.

slides.title: Equivalent Tests For Semi-Simplicity
slides.notes: Frame the equivalences as a conversion chart. Depending on the problem, one test may be visible while another is useful. In geometry, compactness may give reductive representation behavior, while algebraic decomposition may be needed to analyze symmetric pairs or invariant forms.

slides.title: Reductive Means Split Enough
slides.notes: Connect reductivity to compact geometry. When a compact group acts linearly, one can average an inner product and get invariant orthogonal complements. That is why compact isotropy algebras and compact transformation groups repeatedly produce reductive subalgebras in the geometric chapters.

slides.title: Compact Subgroups Give Reductive Subalgebras
slides.notes: This is the geometric proof pattern that students should remember. Compactness is not used abstractly; it supplies averaging. Once an invariant inner product exists, invariant subspaces have invariant complements, and that is exactly the linear-algebra mechanism behind reductivity in compact isotropy situations.

slides.title: Levi Subalgebras Split The Radical
slides.notes: Stress the direction of the theorem. The quotient by the radical is semi-simple automatically, but Levi says one can choose a semi-simple subalgebra inside the original algebra that maps isomorphically onto that quotient. Later symmetric-space arguments need this internal representative.

slides.title: Compact Symmetry Can Preserve A Levi Choice
slides.notes: This slide explains why the appendix proves more than ordinary Levi decomposition. In Chapter XI, an involution or compact automorphism group must preserve the chosen semi-simple complement. The key image is affine averaging: compactness turns a moving family of complements into one invariant complement.

slides.title: The Abelian-Radical Case Is A Cocycle Picture
slides.notes: Do not dwell on cohomology terminology, but let students see the graph construction. When the radical is abelian, changing a Levi complement is the same as choosing a linear correction into the radical. The identity displayed is exactly what makes the graph closed under the bracket.

slides.title: Real Simple Algebras And Complexification
slides.notes: Present the dichotomy as a structural fork. If complexification is not simple, a complex ideal projects isomorphically onto the real algebra and produces the operator J. If no compatible J exists, the complexified algebra must remain simple, which matters when classifying real symmetric Lie algebras.

slides.title: Compact Type Is A Sign Condition
slides.notes: Make the sign condition concrete. Compact adjoint orbits allow an invariant positive inner product, and the adjoint maps become skew-symmetric, making traces of squares non-positive. In the semi-simple case nondegeneracy removes the zero directions, yielding compact type.

slides.title: Real Forms Of Complex Semi-Simple Algebras
slides.notes: Keep this slide at the level needed for the differential-geometry course. The appendix does not develop root systems in detail here, but it records the existence of compact real forms because symmetric-space duality and compact versus noncompact types repeatedly depend on choosing the right real slice.

slides.title: Where The Appendix Enters Geometry
slides.notes: This is the bridge slide back to the main course. The appendix supplies facts that make later proofs shorter: invariant Levi subalgebras for symmetric decompositions, reductive subalgebras from compact isotropy, and sign or nilpotency restrictions for transformation groups of Riemannian and Kahler structures.

slides.title: Instructor Exercise: Preserve The Split
slides.notes: Use this exercise to rehearse the proof strategy without drowning in notation. A finite group generated by an involution is compact, so averaging is legal. The students should say that the action on Levi complements is affine and that the averaged point gives an invariant complement.

slides.title: Summary
slides.notes: Close by returning to the course-level purpose. The appendix gives students the algebraic levers needed later: series for measuring noncommutativity, radicals for isolating solvable pieces, Killing forms for semi-simple tests, and Levi complements for symmetry-compatible decompositions in differential geometry.
